# Forough Mahpouya

<div class="position-line">
Ph.D. Candidate in Industrial and Systems Engineering
</div>

<div class="affiliation-line">
Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering · University at Buffalo
</div>

::: {.bio-text}

I am a Ph.D. candidate in Industrial and Systems Engineering at the University at Buffalo, advised by Dr. Alexander Nikolaev and Dr. Sabrina Casucci, and expect to graduate in June 2027. I am on the academic job market for tenure-track faculty positions in 2026–27.

My research develops causal learning and decision methods for healthcare data shaped by who gets seen: patients who face barriers to care miss visits and leave fewer records, so they are the least visible in the data used to evaluate their care. My doctoral work focuses on aging and caregiving. I developed adversarial balancing representations for treatments measured on a continuous scale and used them to estimate how caregiver burden affects older adults’ transitions into long-term care, along with a measure that separates caregivers’ burden from the benefits of caregiving. A complementary line of work concerns sequential experimentation: identifying the best options while making efficient use of costly comparisons. Next, I will study opioid tapering, asking how taper speed affects patients’ outcomes when follow-up visits are missed, and how to choose a taper speed when outcomes compete.

In teaching, I emphasize the reasoning behind an engineering model: what it represents, which assumptions it relies on, and what conclusions it can support. Through case exercises and peer discussion, students explain their choices, consider alternatives, and revise their work, building the judgment to address unfamiliar problems, including evaluating AI recommendations.

My research appears in *IISE Transactions*, *Health Services and Outcomes Research Methodology* (accepted), and *Quality and Reliability Engineering International*. I received the 2025–2026 University at Buffalo ISE Graduate Student Teaching Award and was selected as an IISE Future Faculty Fellow.

## Research

My research connects causal inference, machine learning, and operations research to improve healthcare decisions when records depend on who gets seen and what gets recorded. Patients who miss visits receive less care, may have worse outcomes, and leave fewer records, so the patients facing the most barriers to care are the least visible in the data used to evaluate it. I develop methods that estimate treatment effects from such incomplete records and use those estimates to guide treatment and care decisions.

### Causal Learning from Observational Health Data
My doctoral research develops adversarial balancing representations for treatments measured on a continuous scale, learning patient summaries that make treatment levels comparable while preserving the information needed to estimate outcomes. Applied to older adults and their unpaid caregivers in linked national surveys, they showed that one-year risk of entering long-term care rises from about 4% at moderate caregiver burden to about 10% at high burden, a pattern that high-versus-low comparisons would hide.

This focus emerged from my systematic review of dementia-management research, which found weaknesses in confounding adjustment and limited attention to caregivers. In that review, I applied PSM-Qual, a scale I co-developed for assessing propensity-score studies. My work on measuring caregiving led to CareBI, an index that represents caregivers' burden and benefit as separate dimensions.


### Sequential Experimentation for Decisions

My first-authored paper in *IISE Transactions* asks how to choose pairwise comparisons so that the best student-created learning materials can be identified with limited evaluation effort. I led the development of a method that prioritizes comparisons by their expected value for identifying the top items, using Markov chain perturbation analysis with error bounds to make selection about 130 times faster for 100 items. The expected value of experimentation now guides how I measure what additional evidence is worth in health decisions.

### Causal Learning When Observation Shapes the Data
My next research direction models who gets seen as part of the causal problem. My first project studies opioid tapering among older adults, where clinicians are advised to follow up at least monthly, yet primary care visits fall after tapers that end with opioids stopped. Using national survey interviews linked to Medicare claims, I will estimate who goes unseen and what records miss, how taper speed affects overdose, mental health crises, and death, and which taper speed each patient should receive when these outcomes compete and the estimates are uncertain. The same approach extends to diabetes care, where glucose testing is more frequent when control is poor, and to drug manufacturing oversight, where inspections target sites already considered risky.

## Teaching

I believe good teaching begins with listening to how students reason and designing activities that make that reasoning visible. In Simulation Modeling and Analysis, I have led recitations and course lectures and developed case-based exercises using Arena and @RISK in which students define systems, identify sources of uncertainty, make modeling choices, and explain what their results do and do not justify. These contributions, together with my broader work in the course, were recognized with the University at Buffalo ISE Graduate Student Teaching Award.

### Probability, Statistics, and Simulation

**EAS 305 — Applied Probability & Statistics**  
Led recitations, designed recitation materials, delivered Minitab laboratory instruction, and conducted exam-review lectures.

**IE 477 — Simulation Modeling and Analysis**

**IE 551 — Simulation and Stochastic Models**  
Delivered course instruction and supported students through group-specific active office hours.

### Manufacturing and Operations

**IE 406/506 — Computer Integrated Manufacturing**  
Led laboratory tutorials using Autodesk Fusion 360 for 3D CAD modeling and manufacturing.

**IE 505 — Production Planning and Control**  
Supported instruction in production-planning and operations topics.

### Health Systems

**IE 585 — Industrial Engineering Principles and Practice in Healthcare**  
Guest lectured on PICO question formulation and analysis of complex observational healthcare datasets.
